title: Misclassification of opioid-involvement in drug-related overdose deaths in the United States: A scoping review

claims.statement: In the places and years studied, official counts missed some drug deaths, mostly because the certificate or its codes named no drug, or not the drug a fuller review identified, and they also included some deaths that a fuller review did not count as drug deaths; how many in each direction depends on the place, the period and the yardstick used. Certificates that name no drug: in US death records for 1999–2015, 23.1% of 568,699 drug poisoning deaths of all intents had no specific drug identified (26.0% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015) (Ruhm, 2018), and 97,159 of 438,607 unintentional overdose deaths (22%) named none, from 0% in Washington DC to 50.8% in Pennsylvania in 2015 (Buchanich et al., 2018); in 2010, 9,429 of 38,329 overdose deaths (about a quarter) carried only the code for unspecified drugs (Slavova et al., 2015). These national records do not show which deaths had toxicology. By 2023 the share of US overdose deaths with no drug or drug-class code had fallen to 4.0%, from 12.3% in 2017 (Garnett et al., 2026, editors' arithmetic), so corrections for 1999–2015 should not be carried to later years. Two corrections assumed that deaths naming no drug involved opioids as often as similar deaths with a named drug: a statistical model raised national opioid-involved counts by 21% to 36% a year (33,091 to about 40,000 in 2015; Ruhm, 2018), and reallocation by state and year added about 70,000 unintentional opioid-related deaths over 1999–2015, 5,662 of them in 2015, doubling Pennsylvania's 2015 rate (Buchanich et al., 2018). Neither was checked against toxicology or case records, both can only add deaths, and the national range of 20% to 35% that a scoping review reports comes from one author's repeated analyses of the same records (Gutkind et al., 2025). Searching the words written on certificates recovers drug names that the codes merge, but not a drug that was never written (Ossiander, 2014; Garnett et al., 2026). Counts can also jump when recording practice changes: as a review reports, South Carolina's death rate from prescription-type opioids went from 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000 between 2013 and 2014, mainly because certificates naming specific drugs rose from 57.7% to 94.4% once the state began collecting drug names (Slavova et al., 2019, second-hand). Studies that compared two counting methods for the same deaths, the strongest evidence here, found gaps in both directions. In the Stockholm area in 1985–1996, a selection of death certificates by drug codes held 761 (63%) of 1,212 deaths in an inventory that assessed each death individually (1,061 of them examined forensically); but the inventory also counted deaths of people with a history of drug use problems whatever the cause, including 151 hospital deaths, mainly HIV-related, under a third of which the certificate selection held, so not every death it missed was a missed poisoning. In the other direction, the certificate selection held 419 deaths that the inventory did not; the authors judged only 30 of them drug-related by the inventory's definition, the rest including drownings after taking medicines and deaths related to alcohol or medicines rather than illegal drugs. Its total (1,181) was therefore close to the inventory's while about a third of the individual deaths differed in each direction; a toxicology-based register held 317 of 454 inventory deaths in 1994–1996, and 43 of its own cases reflected medical treatment rather than illicit use (Fugelstad et al., 2020). In New Mexico in 1995–1998, vital statistics left out 37 deaths that the state medical investigator classed as poisonings (coded as natural deaths because poisoning was written only in Part II of the certificate) and included 15 that the medical investigator classed as natural deaths (coded as drug use because of the certificate's words) (Landen et al., 2003). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, the Office for National Statistics counted a death under a specific opioid only when the coroner's conclusion named it; in coroner-reported cases of a national programme on drug deaths, 29% (2011) to 36% (2022) of heroin or morphine deaths, and similar shares for other opioids, had an ambiguous cause such as multi-drug toxicity with the programme's toxicologist implicating the opioid, and applying those shares to the national counts, without linking the records, gave projected totals of which the official counts held 61% to 68% (13,471 heroin or morphine deaths against a projected 20,323); 96.8% of the programme's opioid-related deaths had several drugs detected (Chen et al., 2025). Heroin is a special case, covered in the answer on heroin deaths. Counts that take every drug written on a certificate as involved, and count a death under each drug, cannot show which drug caused a death involving several (Garnett et al., 2026); in US records for 1999–2015, 45% of unintentional deaths counted as opioid-related also carried another drug's code (Buchanich et al., 2018, editors' calculation). Registers of drug-related deaths also include deaths that were not direct overdoses: of 1,037 accidental deaths that coroners in England and Wales reported to a national register in 2000, the register's researchers judged 802 (77%) direct overdoses and the rest sudden events such as breathing in stomach contents (74), drug toxicity on top of a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and infections (18), without comparing them with official statistics (Webb et al., 2003). Definitions also leave deaths out: US overdose counts exclude long-term effects of drugs (Garnett et al., 2026), and the authors of a Liverpool study argue that the UK and European definitions of the time left out deaths from infections spread by injecting (Beynon et al., 2007). No study read here measured how often stimulants, cannabis or new psychoactive substances are missed or wrongly named on certificates; most of the evidence concerns US opioid deaths before 2016. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: No drug named, US: 23.1% of 568,699 drug poisoning deaths 1999–2015 (26.0% in 2008, 17.2% in 2015; Ruhm, 2018); 97,159 of 438,607 unintentional overdose deaths (22%), 0% (Washington DC) to 50.8% (Pennsylvania) in 2015 (Buchanich et al., 2018); 9,429 of 38,329 in 2010 (Slavova et al., 2015); no drug or drug-class code 12.3% in 2017, 4.0% in 2023 (editors' arithmetic from 87.7% and 96.0%; Garnett et al., 2026). Model corrections (untested assumptions): opioid-involved counts 21% to 36% higher each year, 33,091 to 39,999 in 2015 (Ruhm, 2018); about 70,000 reallocated 1999–2015, 5,662 in 2015, Pennsylvania 9.90 to 20.12 per 100,000 (Buchanich et al., 2018). Same deaths counted two ways: Stockholm 1985–1996, certificate selection held 761 of 1,212 inventory deaths (63%) and 419 deaths outside the inventory, 30 of them judged drug-related; toxicology register 1994–1996, 317 of 454, plus 43 medical-treatment cases (Fugelstad et al., 2020). New Mexico 1995–1998: 37 medical-investigator poisonings coded as natural deaths, 15 medical-investigator natural deaths coded as drug use (Landen et al., 2003). England and Wales 2011–2022, unlinked projection: share of the projection not counted 32% (fentanyl) to 39% (methadone); heroin/morphine 13,471 against 20,323 (Chen et al., 2025). Register composition: 802 of 1,037 accidental deaths direct overdoses (Webb et al., 2003). Second-hand: South Carolina 4.7 to 9.3 per 100,000 (2013–2014) as named drugs rose from 57.7% to 94.4% (Slavova et al., 2019). No intervals for any correction.

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the kind of official who investigates a death changes how drug deaths are counted. In the US, counties served by coroners recorded drug deaths less specifically than counties served by medical examiners in the same states, but the one study of states that replaced coroners with medical examiners found no detectable improvement in how specifically poisoning deaths were coded, and across nine states taken together, without allowing for the state, the association ran the other way; no study checked which records were right. In the US, medical examiners are appointed physicians, usually forensic pathologists, while coroners are elected or appointed officials whose qualifications vary widely (Goldberger et al., 2013). In Kentucky, for example, a coroner must be at least 24 years old and meet residence rules, no training in medicine or forensic pathology is required, and new coroners must complete 40 hours of basic training; of 48 coroners who answered a 2016 survey, 47 held another job, 28 as funeral directors (Quesinberry et al., 2019). In the 2018 census of US offices, about 80% were in coroner systems, coroners or other non-physicians most often decided which deaths were tested (64.7%), and offices serving fewer than 25,000 people less often had access to toxicology (75.1%, against 96.4% of offices serving 250,000 or more) (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025). In surveillance records of 55,430 drug poisoning deaths in nine states in 2019–2021, deaths in coroner counties had higher odds of being recorded as of undetermined intent, rather than as an accident or a suicide, than deaths in medical-examiner counties of the same state and year (odds ratio 1.79, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.27; 1.52 to 1.61 after allowing for county characteristics, recorded investigation steps and the person's age, sex and race); without allowing for the state the odds were lower in coroner counties (0.32; 3.1% against 8.9% recorded as undetermined), which the authors attribute to Maryland, a state with a central medical examiner and many undetermined deaths. An alcohol test was recorded for 58.6% of deaths in coroner counties against 84.5% in medical-examiner counties, while autopsies (about 68% and 67%) and opioid tests (about 80% and 79%) were recorded about equally often (editors' percentages); the type of system was taken from a 2024 listing (Lundberg et al., 2026). A scoping review summarizes, second-hand, three studies that found more certificates naming no drug where coroners certify, one with odds ratios of 1.77 (2014) and 3.87 (2018) for an unclassified overdose death in coroner counties (Gutkind et al., 2025); a commentary quotes an earlier analysis in which 92% of overdose certificates named drugs in states with a central medical examiner, against 62% in states with coroners (Slavova et al., 2015, as cited); and a 2019 review reports that Maryland, a central medical-examiner state, recorded 68% of poisoning deaths as of undetermined intent in 2016, against 1% in Connecticut and Massachusetts (Slavova et al., 2019, as cited). Against this, seven states that switched to a medical examiner system in 1976–1996, compared with seven states that did not, chosen for nearness and similar earlier trends, showed no detectable change in the share of poisoning deaths with a non-specific underlying-cause code (difference-in-differences −0.02 to −0.03, standard errors 0.04 to 0.06, so falls of up to 10 to 14 percentage points from a share near one half could not be ruled out, editors' calculation), in data that ended in 1998 and included poisonings by substances other than drugs (Zaychik, 2024). See the contested question. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Nine US states 2019–2021, undetermined intent in coroner against medical-examiner counties (Lundberg et al., 2026): within state and year, odds ratio 1.79 (1.43–2.27); adjusted 1.52 (1.20–1.95), 1.61 (1.26–2.06), 1.60 (1.25–2.05); pooled without state, 0.32 (0.29–0.35), 558 of 18,232 (3.1%) against 3,329 of 37,198 (8.9%). Alcohol test recorded 58.6% against 84.5% (editors' percentages). Second-hand: unclassified overdose deaths in coroner counties, odds ratios 1.77 (1.08–2.90) in 2014 and 3.87 (2.32–6.46) in 2018 (Gutkind et al., 2025); certificates naming drugs 92% (central medical examiner) against 62% (coroner) (Slavova et al., 2015); undetermined share in 2016, 1% to 68% (Slavova et al., 2019). Seven state switches 1976–1996 (Zaychik, 2024): difference-in-differences in the non-specific share −0.02 (SE 0.04), −0.03 (0.05), −0.02 (0.06); editors' 95% intervals −0.10 to 0.06, −0.13 to 0.07, −0.14 to 0.10. US offices 2018: about 80% in coroner systems; toxicology access 75.1% (small) against 96.4% (large) (Smiley-McDonald et al., 2025).

claims.statement: In the three places studied, official counts built from death certificates or coroners' conclusions named heroin in fewer deaths than a fuller review of the investigation files found (Maryland; Victoria, Australia) or a projection estimated (England and Wales), mainly because morphine (which heroin turns into in the body) or a general term such as mixed drug toxicity was written instead; the fuller reviews used their authors' own definitions, which partly counted heroin markers found in toxicology rather than a judgement that heroin caused the death, and in the one place that looked, a few deaths coded as heroin were judged not to be heroin deaths. In Maryland in 2012–2015, certificates written by the state's medical examiner named heroin in 1,130 overdose deaths, while a protocol built by the state's agencies, which also counted deaths with 6-monoacetylmorphine (a breakdown product of heroin) in toxicology, morphine together with quinine (described as a common heroin additive), or morphine or no named drug on the certificate together with scene evidence of heroin, found 2,182; because the protocol includes every certificate naming heroin, it could only add deaths. Of the 1,052 it added, the certificate named morphine in 804, no specific drug in 193 and another substance in 55. Certificates named heroin in 51.8% (95% CI 49.7 to 53.9) of the protocol's heroin deaths, rising from 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, and less often for people aged 55 or older (41.9%), for women (35.1%) and for Black women (25.9%); the authors note that some of the added deaths, including some of the 55, may not have been heroin deaths (Horon et al., 2018). In Victoria, Australia, in 2012–2013, 243 deaths met the authors' own heroin-attribution model applied to closed coroners' files (toxicology together with the circumstances; 6-acetylmorphine was detected in 180, so 63 rested on morphine findings and circumstances), and the national heroin code was missing from 82 of them, leaving the national count 78 lower (165). Of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin, 37 were not coded as heroin, mostly because of the wording (a general cause with the drugs listed only in a database field, morphine written as the cause, or a complication such as brain injury from lack of oxygen written first); 34 of 39 deaths certified as due to morphine or another opioid and all 5 certified as general drug toxicity lacked the heroin code (coders gave it to the other 5 of these 44, although the coroner had not named heroin), and 20 deaths had no code at all. In the other direction, 4 deaths coded as heroin were judged by the model to have involved heroin only by coincidence (Stam et al., 2019). In England and Wales in 2011–2022, the Office for National Statistics counted 13,471 deaths in which the coroner's conclusion named heroin or morphine; in coroner-reported cases of a national programme on drug deaths, 29% (2011) to 36% (2022) of heroin or morphine deaths had an ambiguous cause with the toxicologist implicating the drug, and applying these shares to the national counts, without linking the records, projects about 20,323, about half as many again (editors' calculation); the median number of drugs detected in these deaths rose from four to six (Chen et al., 2025). A scoping review reports, second-hand, similar shifts in US county reviews: in Allegheny County in 2008–2010, heroin deaths rose from 171 to 245 after review while deaths attributed to morphine fell from 132 to 41 and to codeine from 34 to 5, and in New York City in 2006–2010, 84 of 118 deaths certified as acute opiate intoxication were attributed to heroin (Gutkind et al., 2025). Why heroin is missed, as the authors describe it from the literature: heroin turns quickly into 6-acetylmorphine and then into morphine, so morphine found after death may come from heroin or from morphine itself, and 6-acetylmorphine may not be found after a long interval between use and death or in stored samples (Stam et al., 2019; Horon et al., 2018). US national statistics note that morphine on certificates may reflect heroin, which would understate heroin and overstate morphine (Garnett et al., 2026), and a US medical examiners' position paper treats 6-acetylmorphine as sufficient evidence of heroin and a morphine-to-codeine ratio above 1 as possible evidence, without a cited test of these rules (Davis et al., 2020). None of these studies checked its fuller review against an independent standard, and all concern 2006–2022; whether the deaths added by the reviews were caused by heroin, rather than involving it, is not shown, and what an opioid level after death can show is a separate question. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Maryland 2012–2015 (Horon et al., 2018): 1,130 deaths with heroin on the certificate against 2,182 by the enhanced protocol (28.6% and 55.1% of 3,957 overdose deaths, a total not defined in the paper); added 1,052: morphine certified 804, no specific drug 193, other substance 55; certificates named heroin in 51.8% (49.7–53.9) of protocol deaths, 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015); 41.9% at 55 or older, 35.1% of women, 25.9% (18.5–33.3) of Black women. Victoria 2012–2013 (Stam et al., 2019): 243 model-defined deaths (6-acetylmorphine in 180) against 165 with the heroin code; code missing from 82 (34%, editors' arithmetic); 4 coded deaths judged coincidental; coroner-attributed heroin deaths coded 154 of 191; morphine or other opioid certified 5 of 39 coded; generic 0 of 5; 20 with no code. England and Wales 2011–2022 (Chen et al., 2025; unlinked projection): ONS 13,471 against 20,323 projected (about 51% more, editors' calculation); 2011 574 against 813 (95% CI 767–868); 2022 1,264 against 1,980. Second-hand (Gutkind et al., 2025): Allegheny County heroin 171 to 245, morphine 132 to 41, codeine 34 to 5; New York City 84 of 118 opiate-intoxication deaths attributed to heroin. Reference standards unvalidated; no intervals for the Victorian or projected counts.
